questions.q: Per this lesson, what does it mean when a multi-org landscape is 'accidental rather than designed'?
options: It means the orgs were created through a deliberate, documented strategic decision
It means orgs accumulated through events like mergers, acquisitions, or independent regional implementations, without central coordination
It means Salesforce automatically creates a second org after a certain number of users
It means the company has never used Salesforce before
questions.explain: The lesson describes accidental multi-org as arising from mergers/acquisitions bringing in separate orgs or regional divisions implementing independently, without central coordination -- as opposed to a deliberate strategic choice.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in this lesson as a legitimate factor favoring multiple orgs?
options: Isolation and compliance -- keeping data cleanly separated where regulatory requirements or sensitivity profiles differ
Guaranteed lower total licensing cost in every case
Automatic elimination of all systems-of-record problems
Simplified cross-business-unit reporting
questions.explain: Isolation and compliance is listed as a real factor favoring multiple orgs; the lesson actually lists cost and simplified cross-business reporting as factors favoring a SINGLE org, and explicitly says multi-org recreates systems-of-record problems rather than eliminating them.

questions.q: What does this lesson say a 'Reference Architecture' is, in the multi-org context?
options: A technical diagram of Salesforce's own internal server infrastructure
A documented decision framework, defined in advance by the governance body, stating when an additional org is reasonable or necessary
A specific Salesforce sandbox type used for testing
The org that was created first, which automatically becomes authoritative over all others
questions.explain: A Reference Architecture is the governance body's documented, in-advance decision framework for when creating an additional org is actually justified, so the question doesn't get re-litigated informally every time it comes up.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens to the systems-of-record problem from Lesson 3 in a multi-org architecture?
options: It disappears entirely, since all orgs run the same Salesforce platform
It recurs -- two orgs both claiming authority over the same customer's data is the same dueling-systems-of-record failure, just within the same platform's logo
It only applies to non-Salesforce systems, never between two Salesforce orgs
It is automatically resolved by Salesforce's built-in cross-org sync feature
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states multi-org recreates the dueling-systems-of-record failure -- two orgs both claiming to be authoritative for the same entity is the same underlying problem, just occurring between two orgs on the same platform.

questions.q: Which question does this lesson list as one that helps separate a justified multi-org decision from an accidental one?
options: What color scheme does each business unit prefer for its Salesforce theme?
Are the business units essentially unrelated, with separate P&Ls, or deeply interdependent?
How many Trailhead badges have the business unit's admins earned?
Which business unit was founded first?
questions.explain: The lesson lists whether business units are essentially unrelated with separate P&Ls, alongside standardized-process alignment and cross-business reporting need, as the key questions that distinguish a justified multi-org decision from an accidental one.
